lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: Albert Einstein is famous for relativity... and E equals m c squared. But his Nobel Prize wasn't for either of them.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: [intrigued] It was for something smaller. Something that changed what we think light actually is.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: In nineteen oh five, Einstein was a twenty-six-year-old patent clerk in Switzerland. That year, he published four papers that would reshape physics. One of them explained a strange little puzzle called the photoelectric effect.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: Here's the puzzle. Shine light on a metal, and sometimes electrons come flying out of it.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: At the time, everyone agreed light was a wave. So the obvious prediction was: brighter light means a stronger wave, which should knock electrons out with more energy.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: But that's not what happened. Blast the metal with bright red light... and nothing. Not a single electron.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: Now shine a dim violet light. [surprised] Electrons pop out instantly.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: Make the violet light brighter, and you get more electrons... but each one has the same energy. Only changing the color changes their speed. Waves couldn't explain any of this.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: Einstein's answer was radical. Light isn't just a smooth wave. It comes in tiny packets of energy. Today, we call them photons.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: And the energy of each packet depends on its color. Red photons carry a little energy. Violet photons carry a lot.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: Think of it like trying to break a window. Throw a million ping-pong balls, and the glass survives. Throw one baseball, and it shatters.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: One photon hits one electron. If the photon has enough energy to pay the exit fee, the electron escapes. If not, it doesn't matter how many photons you send.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: Einstein wrote it as one simple equation. The electron's energy equals the photon's energy, minus the cost of escaping the metal.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: Plenty of physicists didn't buy it. The American physicist Robert Millikan spent about ten years testing it, fully expecting it to fail. [beat] It didn't. His measurements matched Einstein's equation.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: So in nineteen twenty-two, Einstein received the nineteen twenty-one Nobel Prize in Physics, especially for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect. Relativity was still considered too controversial.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: [amused] Two fun details. The prize money went to his ex-wife, Mileva, as agreed in their divorce. And when he gave his Nobel lecture... he talked about relativity anyway.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: But the real prize was the idea. Light behaving as a particle helped launch quantum physics, the strange rules that govern atoms.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: And it's in your life every day. Camera sensors, light sensors, and solar panels all rely on light knocking electrons loose, one photon at a time.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: [warm] Einstein's most famous ideas are about space and time. But his Nobel Prize was for showing us what light is made of.

lines.speaker: nar
lines.text: If you learned something, subscribe. And tell me in the comments: which famous discovery should we visualize next?
